Transcript:
A brain scan finishes at an Alaska hospital. Every minute without blood flow, about two million brain cells die.
Before, just sending those images to Anchorage could take forty-five minutes.
Now a volunteer group, the Alaska Stroke Coalition, has hospitals using A I software called RapidAI.
It looks for a large vessel occlusion, a clot blocking a big brain artery.
In one case, it alerted the doctor seconds after the scan.
The results reached the local team and the clot specialists at once.
That speed counts. The whole state has five doctors who can pull out those clots.
In another case, a man in his sixties fell and came into a hospital in Alaska's interior.
Less than half an hour after he arrived, his team called Providence in Anchorage for a transfer.
That call came two minutes before the official scan report.
Four hours and twenty-three minutes after he arrived, the clot was out.
The information moves ahead of the patient. Early, unpublished data shows about a thirty percent faster start on clot removal once patients reach Anchorage.
Now the hard part. Kelly Isaacs, who manages Providence's stroke program, says she can't really show statistically significant proof it's made a big difference.
Alaska doesn't have consistent reporting of stroke outcomes. The software throws false positives.
The clinicians answer that a doctor reviews every output, and that read decides the transfer.
Six hospitals that got it free all say they want to keep it and pay for it.
Over three point one million dollars in federal rural health money is set to build an A I imaging network across twenty-one hospitals, Utqiagvik to Juneau.
The alert can already beat the paperwork. What should Alaska measure to know it's working?
